en: Petavatthu, Uragavagga 5. Tirokuṭṭapetavatthu The Story of the Ghost Who Passes Through Walls Once upon a time, monks, there was a certain householder in Sāvatthī who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast means, with abundant gold, silver, bullion, and treasures, and many possessions and assets. He had a son who was dear and beloved to him. Then, monks, that householder fell ill, was gravely ill, and lay on his deathbed. To him, his son said: "Father, give me your inheritance. "I have no wealth to give you, my son," he replied. "Father, give me your wealth; give me your wealth! the son urged him again and again. "Son, I have no wealth to give you," the father said. "But, my son, there is a certain ghost here in this very house who possesses great wealth and vast means, with abundant gold, silver, bullion, and treasures, and many possessions and assets. Go to him and say: 'Sir, please give me your wealth. Then, monks, the son went to that ghost and said: "Sir, please give me your wealth. "My son, I have no wealth to give you," the ghost replied. "But, my son, there is a certain ghost here in the next room who possesses great wealth and vast means, with abundant gold, silver, bullion, and treasures, and many possessions and assets. “They stand at the walls,
and at the junctions and crossroads;
they stand at the doorposts.”
Having returned to his own home,
where abundant food and drink,
as well as various kinds of snacks and meals, were set out;
No one remembers them,
due to the condition of karma for living beings.
Thus they give to their relatives.
Those who are compassionate give pure,
excellent, and permissible food and drink at the proper time.
‘May this be for your kinsmen;
may your kinsmen be happy.
And they, having gathered there, [said:]
The departed relatives have assembled;
amidst abundant food and drink,
they offer their sincere appreciation.
“May our relatives live long,
for whose sake we receive these things;
and may the honor they have paid us [bear fruit].”
And the donors are not without fruit.
For there is no plowing there,
nor is cattle-rearing found there.
There is no trade like this:
buying and selling with gold;
by what is given from here, they maintain themselves.
The departed ones who have passed away there are like water rained upon a high ground that flows down to the lowlands.
In this very way, what is given from here benefits the departed;
just as rivers full of water, when swollen, flow toward the great ocean.
They fill the ocean;
even so, what is given from here benefits the departed spirits.
"He gave to me, he did for me,
he was my kinsman, friend, and companion"— with such thoughts,
one should give an offering to the departed.
Recalling what was done in the past:
for neither weeping nor sorrow,
nor any other lamentation, [averts the past].
That does not benefit the departed;
thus do kinsmen stand.
But this gift that has been given—
Well-established within the Saṅgha,
it serves for one’s welfare for a long time,
providing benefit according to the occasion.
Thus has this duty toward kinsmen been demonstrated,
and a sublime offering made to the departed;
and strength has been bestowed upon the monks.
“By you, a vast and inexhaustible merit has been performed.
The Fifth Story of the Petas Visible Through Walls.
